hil eius iugum subterfugit: quo contemptus idignet atque irascat, nec est sapientius eo quicquid illi emulationem incutiat. Itaque cum hec illi non accidant: nihil eius nature preter ipsum bonum restat. Quemadmodum vero nihil eorum que mala sunt in hac sunt effeta: ita in nullo alio bonum inuenitur. In singulis enim reliqua sunt singula: tum in paruis tum in magnis tum etiam in his que secundum unum et in ipso quoque animali maximo omnium atque potentissimo quod utique passionibus genita replet. Nam gnatio: passio quedam est, ubi autem passio: nullo modo bonum, ubi bonum: non passio ponitur ulla. ubi dies: nullo modo nox: ubi nox neque etiam dies, Quapropter in generatione bonum esse non potest. restat itaque eo quod ingenitum. Vt autem materie concessa est omnium participatio: sic quoque boni participatione mundus bonus, bonum dico: in quantum ipse etiam omnia efficit, qua quidem ex parte bonus est mundus: in reliquis omnibus non bonus, passibilis ei ac mobilis est: et omnium preterea causa passionum. In homine insuper comparatione mali: bonum. Id quippe quod non nimis malum quoque minus malum: bonum in hominibus appellamus. Quofit: ut bonum nostrum nihil aliud sit quam mali portio minima. Vnde illud etiam sequitur: ut bonum huiusmodi a malo separatum esse non possit, Inquinat enim hoc bonum: admixtione malorum. infectum vero ulterius bonum non permanet, sin minime permanet: malum efficit. In solo igitur deo bonum ipsum existit. Quare solum boni nomen homini adesto Esculapi: natura boni nequaquam, neque enim id capere potest materiale corpus confectum undique et oppressum prauitate, laboribus, doloribus, cupiditatibus, iracundia, deceptionibus, stultisque opinionibus, ac nugis. Deterrimum tamen omnium id censeo Esculapi: quod unum quodque eorum que dixi: summum creditur esse bonum. Fugiendum in primis malum est, uentris luxus: malorum omnium fomes, hic

escapes His yoke, at which, being despised, He might be indignant and grow angry. Nor is there anything wiser than Him that might strike emulation into Him. Therefore, since these things do not happen to Him, nothing remains of His nature except the good itself. Just as, however, none of those things that are evil are contained in Him, so the good is not found in any other. For in individuals, other things are individuals, both in small things, in great things, and even in those which are according to one, and in that greatest and most powerful animal of all, which indeed fills the things begotten with passions. For generation is a certain passion; where there is passion, however, the good is not placed in any way. Where there is good, no passion is placed. Where there is day, there is in no way night; where there is night, neither is there day. Therefore, the good cannot exist in generation. It remains, therefore, that it is in that which is unbegotten. Just as, however, participation in all things is granted to matter, so also the world is good by participation in the good; I say good, in so far as it also makes all things. In which part the world is indeed good; in all remaining things, it is not good. For it is passive and movable, and furthermore the cause of all passions. In man, moreover, by comparison to evil, it is good. For that which is not too much evil, but also less evil, we call good among men. From which it happens that our good is nothing other than the smallest portion of evil. From where it also follows that the good of this kind cannot be separated from evil. For this good pollutes with the admixture of evils; the good, however, does not remain further infected. If it does not remain at all, it makes evil. In God alone, therefore, does the good itself exist. Wherefore, let the name of the good be present to man alone, O Asclepius; the nature of the good, by no means. For the material body, finished everywhere and oppressed by depravity, labors, pains, desires, wrath, deceptions, and foolish opinions and trifles, cannot grasp it. I consider it the worst of all, however, O Asclepius, that each one of those things which I have said is believed to be the highest good. Evil must be avoided in the first place; the luxury of the belly is the tinder of all evils, this

Equidem ingentes deo gratias habeo: qui de natura boni cogitati mihi sententiam hanc certam infudit, quod in mundo bonum esse non possit. siquidem mundus congeries est malorum. Deus autem boni vel boni dei exuberans plenitudo. supereminentia quippe bonorum circa essentiam sincere fulgentis atque purissime. Neque forte sunt essentie dei. Audiendum sane id affero o Esculapi: essentiam dei (si ullam deus habet essentiam) ipsum bonum esse. Pulchrum vero et bonum in mundo: aut in mundi partibus inuenire non licet. Nam quecunque sensus mouet: idola sunt et vane quedam admirationes, que vero sensuum organa subterfugiunt: ad pulchrum bonumque ptinent. Vtque acies oculi deum non cernit: sic neque pulchrum bonumque cognoscit. He siquidem partes dei sunt: integerrimique illius proprie cognate inseparabiles precipueque dilecte, et vt has ipse deus amat: sic ab his ipse deus amatur, si deum percipere poteris: pulchrum quoque bonumque percipies, perfulges oibus illustratu a deo. Pulchritudo enim sine comparatione sine imitatione bonum, Deus ei copatione imitationeque nulla admittit. Quemadmodum ergo deum pulchrum bonumque noueris: ita sane et ceteris viuentibus cum deo conferri nequeant nunquam communicandum. Si deum quiſieris: pulchritudine ipsa qres. Que tandem ad id ferat: vnica via est, pietas cognitioni coniuncta. Quapropter ignari mortales et a pietatis semita deuij: hominem quoque bonum noiare non veretur, cum boni noticia vera habere nulla possit, sed malis irretitus et illaqueatus sit, malumque bonum esse ceseat, insanabiliterque malis vtat, eorumque iactura priuationeque formidet, oibus denique machinametis viribusque cotedat, ne vnico solu malo prematur, vere et in numerose mala magnitudineque augeatur. Talia fut o Esculapi decora ho

error, hence the privation of the good. I truly have great thanks to God, who has infused into me this certain sentiment concerning the nature of the good, that the good cannot exist in the world. For the world is a heap of evils. God, however, is the overflowing plenitude of the good or of the good God, the supereminence of good things indeed shining sincerely and most purely around the essence. Nor are they, perhaps, the essences of God. I truly bring this to be heard, O Asclepius: that the essence of God (if God has any essence) is the good itself. But it is not permitted to find the beautiful and the good in the world or in the parts of the world. For whatever moves the senses are idols and certain vain admirations, but those things which escape the organs of the senses pertain to the beautiful and the good. And just as the sharpness of the eye does not discern God, so it does not know the beautiful and the good. For these are parts of God, properly cognate, inseparable, and especially loved by His most entire self. And as God Himself loves these, so God Himself is loved by them. If you can perceive God, you will also perceive the beautiful and the good. You shine through all things, illuminated by God. For beauty is the good without comparison and without imitation. God admits of no comparison and imitation. Just as, therefore, you will know God to be beautiful and good, so indeed, it should never be communicated to other living things, since they cannot be compared with God. If you will seek God, you will seek beauty itself. What, finally, may lead to that, there is only one way: piety joined to knowledge. Wherefore, ignorant mortals, and those straying from the path of piety, do not fear to name man good also, although he can have no true knowledge of the good, but is entangled and ensnared by evils, and believes evil to be good, and uses evils incurably, and fears the loss and privation of them, and finally contends with all machines and powers, so that he may not be pressed by one evil alone, and may be increased in true and numerous evils and in magnitude. Such, O Asclepius, are the decorations of man

Extus hoc contedit. in solo deo bonu/bonique natura (hoc est ipsa bonitate) reperiri: pariter et pulchri potestis sapientisque natura. In mundo autem solum boni nomen est. et error cecos homines arguit. vicia abhorrere monet. et quae via nos ad ipsa bonitate/ipsaque pulchritudine perducat/edocet/pietas scilicet cognitioni coniuncta. ad qua ignari mortales a pietatis semita deuii: pertingere valeant nunquam. Hec sextus.

Quod summum malu est hominibus ignorare deum. VII

<margin>q</margin>
Voruitis mortales ebrii: qui meru ignorantie bibistis. cum id ferre neqatis: euomite. Viuite sobrii: oculis mentis inspicite. Quod si minus potestis: saltem qui possunt id agant. Ignorantie pestis omnem terram subuertit/animamque corrumpit/corporis vinclis inclusa: neque sinit eam salutis iter asciscere. ne permittite vos in lacu corruptionis/mortisque submergi. Respirate iam respirate/ad fonte vite recurrite: illumque qui vos introducet in adytum veritatis/capescite. ibi fulgidum lumen nullis immixtu tenebris. ibi nullus ebrietate delirat sed omnes sobrii vigilant: atque mentis oculis eum/qui videri vult/acutius intuentur. Is nec auribus percipitur/nec cernitur oculis/neque sermone profertur: sola mens eum prospicit/sola mens predicat. In primis autem oportet veste/qua circumfers: exuere indumentu inicitie/prauitatis fundamentu/corruptionis vinculum/velamen opacum/viuam mortem/sensituum cadauer/sepulchru circumertile/domesticum denique furem. Qui dum blanditur: odit. dum odit: iuidet. huiuscemodi est: quo circumtegeris vmbraculu inimicum. Ad seipsum te deorsum raptat: ne forte cons

and good things, which we can neither flee nor hate. For this is most difficult of all, and for this reason especially: because it is necessary for us to use and partake of them, and deprived of them we could in no way lead our lives.

<margin>f</margin>
The sixth <note>section/chapter</note> contends with this. In God alone can the good, the nature of the good (which is goodness itself), and likewise the nature of the beautiful and the wise be found. In the world, however, there is only the name of the good; and error proves men blind, warns them to abhor vices, and teaches what path may lead us to goodness itself and beauty itself—namely, piety joined to knowledge. Ignorant mortals, straying from the path of piety, can never attain this. This is the sixth.

That it is the greatest evil for men to be ignorant of God. VII

<margin>q</margin>
Drunken mortals, you who have drunk the wine of ignorance, since you cannot bear it, vomit it up. Live soberly; look with the eyes of the mind. But if you cannot, at least let those who can do so. The plague of ignorance overturns the whole earth, corrupts the soul enclosed in the bonds of the body, and does not permit it to choose the path of salvation. Do not allow yourselves to be submerged in the lake of corruption and death. Breathe now, breathe; return to the fountain of life, and take hold of Him who will introduce you into the sanctuary of truth. There shines a brilliant light, unmixed with any darkness. There no one wanders in drunkenness, but all are sober and vigilant, and with the eyes of the mind they behold Him more keenly—He who wishes to be seen. He is neither perceived by the ears, nor seen by the eyes, nor expressed in speech; the mind alone looks upon Him, the mind alone proclaims Him. But first, you must strip off the garment you wear: the foundation of malice, the bond of corruption, the opaque veil, the living death, the corpse of the senses, the mobile sepulcher, and finally, the domestic thief. Who, while he fancies you, hates you; while he hates you, he envies you. Such is the enemy shade by which you are covered. It drags you downward to itself, so that you might not by chance look

pages.translation:
The nations exult with merit, and we, now easy prey,
Are to the Bistones and the snowy tribes.
The rising expanse will grow foul, the plows having been driven out.
Alas for me, what cities, and in what time of Mars,
Ignorant of war, they have seized in a single course!
Recently, the cavalry coming from the furthest Araxes
Terrified the walls of Antioch: and the very head of beautiful
Syria was nearly consumed by hostile flames.
And as it rushes, heavy with spoils, and with nothing hindering,
Happy in the slaughter: the continuous wound follows
With a second blade: nor does the Caucasus now send me enemies,
Nor does the icy Phasis: wars are born in the very
Bosom. The Roman legion of old, the Gothunni
To whom we gave rights when conquered; to whom we provided
Fields and homes; they lay waste to the Lydians and the richest parts of Asia
With fires: and if any part remained from the first tempest.
Relying on neither leader nor number, but sloth nourishes them,
A prodigy of leaders: through whose crimes the captive soldier
Turns his back to his own: those whom I subdued with the
Danube as witness: and he fears a part, who repelled them all.
The court is empty of dances and feasts: nor do they care for what is lost:
While something remains. Yet, lest the seller lose anything
With the world cut to pieces. Every surviving province
Is divided: and about to suffer the double tribunal,
It is forced to make up the price of the destroyed one in turns.
Thus they restore the peoples to me. By this art, they find
Ways to increase the number of rulers while the lands perish.
In you now is my only hope. Instead of the leaf of Minerva,
I hold out these tears to you. Succor the falling.
Snatch me away at last. Snatch me away from servile kingdoms.

pages.translation:
Nor should you condemn everyone for the crimes of a few:
Nor let a new offense stand in the way of so many previous merits.
Now, now bend your mind. Final dangers always
Grant pardon to a fault. Though angry and an exile,
Camillus did not delay his arms for the sake of his country's flames.
We do not withdraw you from Latium as a defender; you are
Sufficient for both. Let it be permitted to enjoy the splendor
Of your arms in common. Let the same shield protect us:
And let one virtue labor for the twin axis.

CL. CLAUDIAN ON THE PRAISES OF STILICHO, BOOK FIRST.

May the gods continue the Roman joys with full 
favor: and increase success with new successes.

The palace had not yet silenced the festive songs 
of the wedding: it sang of triumphs with Gildo routed:
And the laurel succeeded the warm garlands of the bridal chamber:
So that the prince might receive both the name of husband
And the honor of victor, in equal measure. After the battles of Libya, the crime 
of the East collapsed: and once the Orient was subdued, 
the axes of the consul rise up, defended by Stilicho.
The vows proceed in order. Indeed, if I should hope to heap
The piles of such great deeds into a single song:
I would more readily place Pelion upon icy Ossa.
If I should wish to keep silent about a part: whatever I might leave out:

pages.translation:
It will be meager. I will follow the ancient deeds and your first youth:
The present leads the mind to itself.
I might narrate justice. The glory of Mars shines out.
I might recount the strengths of the armed man. He did more unarmed.
That Latium flourishes. That Africa, restored to Latium, serves:
That Iberia does not know the neighboring Moor:
That Gaul, safe, marvels at the unwarlike Rhine.
Shall I sing of the Thracian Angelida, and the labored struggles
With the Hebrus as witness? A great sea is opened to me:
And the Pierian chariots themselves grow weary with the steep
Road of countless praises. For indeed, ever since
The earth began to be tilled by mortals: never has a pure
Lot of good things been granted to any man. Whom a face honors:
Manners disgrace. Whom a more beautiful soul adorns:
The body abandons. That one is more distinguished in wars:
But he fouls peace with vices. Fortunate in public matters:
But less so in private. Single things ennoble each one:
One is favored by handsome form, one by strength in arms,
One by rigor, one by piety, another by skill in law,
One by offspring, and chaste marriage beds are scattered among all:
In you they flow mixed together: and what separate things
Make men blessed: you hold collected. Why should I revolve deeds?
And the military service of a father? Whose fame, if he had
Done nothing famous: and his faithful right hand had not led
The red-haired wings in strength: would be enough for his son Stilicho.
An arduous mind always, even from a boy, and it shone in tender years.
The honor of a greater fortune. Upright, and keen,
To attempt nothing short: to cling to no thresholds
Of the powerful: and already speaking things worthy of future annals:

Abstinence from food is very often a remedy. Thus the Gaul, or Pythagoras, said to Micyllus, who was living frugally: ⁶ "The labors that sharpen you make you a contender not to be despised against those things which seem impregnable to very many. And hence it happens that none of these more serious diseases lays traps for you. But if ever a slight fever has invaded, you medicate it with little trouble and shake it off by fasting. ### CHAP. II.

### *The etymology of the Plague, its names, definition, causes, signs, symptoms, prognostics, forewarnings, preservation, and cure. The diet of those seized by the plague.*

<margin>Names and etymology of the Plague.</margin>
Since there is also a pestilential fever, or rather, since the Plague itself so frequently has fever as a companion that many determine they differ only in the degree of putrefaction, it is worthwhile to discuss it here after the doctrine of fevers. The Plague, which Lucretius also calls pestilence, and which is commonly <margin>¹ Isidore, 5. Etymologies.</margin>¹ called <term>pestilentia</term> <gloss>pestilence</gloss>, as if it were <term>pastilentia</term> <gloss>a feeding-sickness</gloss>, because it devours cities and peoples like a wild, venomous, or <margin>² Galen on Theriac.</margin>² enraged wolf. According to Muretus, it is from the Greek <term>apo tou pesein</term> <gloss>from falling</gloss>. To others, <margin>³ Fr. Junius, 2. Parallels 44.</margin>³ the name <term>pestis</term> <gloss>plague</gloss> is formed by syncope from the compound <term>perestis</term>, changing the *r* into *s* (as is often done) to <term>pesestis</term>, from the verb <term>peredo</term> <gloss>to devour</gloss>; by which is signified whatever eats through, plainly consumes, and destroys any substance. In Greek, it is called <term>loimos</term>, <term>loime</term>, and <term>loigos</term>. <margin>⁴ Eustathius on Iliad 1.</margin>⁴ <term>Loimos</term> is derived either from <term>leipo</term>, which means to fail, according to the notion of the ancients, whence also <term>loimeos</term>, or rather from <term>lecho</term>, <term>lexon</term>, which is to fall asleep into death, but especially from <term>oligou</term>, which means few, with the letter <term>o</term> removed, as if it renders the living few. <margin>⁵ Etymology.</margin>⁵ It is called <term>loimos</term> as if it were <term>loipos</term> from <term>leipo</term>, or from <term>lian</term> and <term>maein</term>, which means to inquire and investigate too much, because it leaves nothing untouched but follows all the traces of hidden things, with the letter <term>o</term> added by pleonasm; or from <term>limos</term> <gloss>hunger</gloss> because of their similarity, for hunger is a lack of food, and plague is a lack of bodies; or rather because of the cause, for <term>ek limou loimos</term> <gloss>from hunger, plague</gloss>. # DE IMAGINIBVS.

->*Quid sunt imagines?*<-

Sunt notæ et formæ quædam, et similitudines earum rerum, quas meminisse volumus.

->*Quot sunt diuisiones imaginum?*<-

->Tres.<-

->*Quæ est prima imaginum diuisio?*<-

Quædam sunt firmæ, et admodum idoneæ; vt sunt res magnæ, incredibiles, inuisæ, inauditæ, nouæ, raræ admirabiles, habentes singularem, vel venustatem, vel turpitudinem. Vel quæ sunt ridiculæ, vel obscenæ. Quædam sunt infirmæ et imbecilles, quæ vix excitare memoriam possunt; vt sunt res paruæ, vsitatæ, quotidianæ. Nam iuxta naturam, quantò res animum nostrum minùs commouerit, tantò citiùs labitur ex memoria. Contrà, quantò fortiùs mouerit, tantò diutiùs et firmiùs memoriæ permanebit impressa.

pages.translation:
# ON IMAGES.

-> *What are images?* <-

They are certain signs and forms, and likenesses of those things which we wish to remember.

-> *How many divisions of images are there?* <-

-> Three. <-

-> *What is the first division of images?* <-

Some are firm and quite suitable; such as things that are large, incredible, ugly, unheard of, new, rare, admirable, having a singular beauty or foulness. Or things which are ridiculous or obscene. Some are weak and feeble, which can scarcely stir the memory; such as things that are small, habitual, and daily. For according to nature, the less a thing has moved our mind, the more quickly it slips from memory. Conversely, the more strongly it has moved it, the longer and more firmly it will remain impressed upon the memory.

*Quae est secunda imaginum diuisio?*

Imagines aliæ sunt rerum, aliæ verborum.

Res sunt duplices: visibiles & invisibiles, corporales & incorporales.

Corporalium, aliæ substantiæ, aliæ accidentia. Voces similiter sunt duplices, quædam notæ, quædam ignotæ.

*Quae est tertia diuisio imaginum?*

Imaginum, aliæ sunt simplices, vt dictionum, aliæ compositæ, vt sententiarum.

*Quae sunt imagines dictionum?*

Quando vna quæque figuratur speciali imagine, vt homo, equus, asinus, suas habent imagines.

*Quae dicuntur imagines sententiarum?*

Quando rem gestam, aut orationem ex pluribus dictionibus compositam, aut totam sententiam, historiam, fabulam, vel carmen vna imagine, vel pluribus comprehendimus: vt, quælibet plaga Ægypti habet suam imaginem, vel ranas, vel locustas.

# ON THE ART

*What is the second division of images?*

Images are either of things or of words.

Things are twofold: visible and invisible, corporeal and incorporeal.

Of corporeal things, some are substances, others are accidents. Voices are likewise twofold: some known, some unknown.

*What is the third division of images?*

Of images, some are simple, such as those for individual words; others are composite, such as those for sentences.

*What are images of words?*

When each individual word is figured by a special image, such as a man, a horse, or an ass, each having its own image.

*What are called images of sentences?*

When we grasp a completed action, or an oration composed of several words, or an entire sentence, history, fable, or poem with one or more images: for example, each plague of Egypt has its own image, whether it be frogs or locusts.

-><-

### *Da conditiones imaginum?*

1. Omnis imago debet esse mirabilis, iucunda, ridicula, crudelis, aut alia insigni passione adfecta. Tales enim imagines plus mouent memorantem, & fortiùs imprimuntur.

2. Imagines non debent esse ociosæ. Quæ enim exercitio carent, parùm vel nihil mouent.

3. Imagines debent esse propriæ, ut rem memorandam repræsentent. Hinc dissimilitudo imaginum vitanda est.

pages.translation:
# REMINISCENCES.

### *Give the conditions of images.*

1. Every image ought to be marvelous, pleasant, ridiculous, cruel, or affected by some other notable passion. For such images move the person memorizing more, and are imprinted more strongly.

2. Images should not be idle. For those which lack activity move little or nothing at all.

3. Images ought to be appropriate, so that they represent the thing to be remembered. Hence, the unlikeness of images is to be avoided.

4. Many images should not be in one and the same place. For they generate confusion. Many images signifying one thing, however, can be placed in one location: for example, for war, many men fighting.

5. Images are invented for the sake of things to be remembered, just as locations are for the sake of order.

6. Images ought to be repeated frequently, so that they are imprinted more firmly. For weakness of impression hinders memory.

<margin>b Paragraph: "therefore when anyone" in the Institutes under this title; Law: "if anyone absent." Paragraph: "in the beginning" in the Digest on obligations and actions; Law 1 in the Digest on actions performed (negotiorum gestio).</margin>
Among these, first offers itself the obligation born mutually from the fact that someone has managed the business of another without his mandate <note>original: "b"</note>.

<margin>c the said Paragraph: "therefore"; Law 2 in the Digest on actions performed.</margin>
2. In which case, a direct action is available against the manager, so that he may render an account of his actions <note>original: "c"</note>.

<margin>d the said Law 2 in the Digest on actions performed.</margin>
3. And on that account he may be condemned, if he has managed anything either not as he ought, or if he retains something from this business <note>original: "d"</note>.

<margin>e the said Paragraph: "therefore"; Law: "if your mother" 24 in the Code on interest.</margin>
4. Since he ought to provide the most exact diligence, provided that someone else would have managed the business more advantageously than he <note>original: "e"</note>.

<margin>f Law 3, Paragraph: "sometimes" in the Digest on actions performed.</margin>
5. For if he offered himself to manage the business compelled by the highest affection, it is most equitable that he be held liable only for deceit <note>original: "f"</note>.

<margin>g Law: "if business" 11 in the Digest on actions performed; it makes the case: Law "if a ward," Law 6, Paragraph "but also if anyone's business" in the Digest on actions performed; Mynsinger in the said Paragraph: "therefore" number 14.</margin>
6. Just as, conversely, a fortuitous case is sometimes provided for, for example, if new business is managed in the name of the absent person, which he is not accustomed to doing <note>original: "g"</note>.

<margin>h the said Paragraph: "therefore"; the said Law 2 at the end in the Digest on actions performed.</margin>
7. A contrary action is available to him who managed it usefully, for whatever is lacking to him on that account, or will be lacking <note>original: "h"</note>.

<margin>i Law: "if however" 8, end of paragraph in the Digest on actions performed; the final law in the Code on the same.</margin>
8. Which, however, is by no means granted to him who managed it against the wish of the owner <note>original: "i"</note>.

<margin>k Paragraph: "tutors" in the Institutes on obligations which arise as if from contract; the said Law 8, paragraph: "guardianship also" in the Digest on obligations and actions.</margin>
9. Similar to the former is that obligation which descends from the administration of guardianship <note>original: "k"</note>.

<margin>l In the beginning in the Digest on guardianship and the distribution of accounts; Law: "whatever" in the Code on the discretion of guardianship.</margin>
10. From it arises a direct action of guardianship, so that the tutor may render an account of his actions, by providing for deceit, fault, and the same diligence as in his own affairs <note>original: "l"</note>.

<margin>m the said Law 1, paragraph: "this action" in the Digest on guardianship and the distribution of accounts; the said Law 1, paragraph: "this action"; Law 1 in the Code on the heir of tutors and curators.</margin>
11. And this is competent to the ward and his heir, against the tutors and their heirs <note>original: "m" and "n"</note>.

<margin>o the said Law 1, paragraph: "let us now treat" in the Digest on guardianship and the distribution of accounts; Law 23 in the Code on dividing guardianship.</margin>
12. By observing the benefit of division and order, if there are several tutors <note>original: "o"</note>.

<margin>p Law 1, paragraph 5, title in the Digest on contrary guardianship and useful action; the said paragraph: "tutors" in the Institutes on obligations which arise as if from contract.</margin>
13. A contrary action is granted to the tutor, to recover that for which the ward is obligated to him from the administration <note>original: "p"</note>.

<margin>q Law 1, paragraph: "in guardianship" in the Digest on guardianship and the distribution of accounts.</margin>
14. From one and the same obligation there is also the action concerning the distribution of accounts <note>original: "q"</note>.

<margin>r Law 2, in the beginning in the Digest on guardianship and the distribution of accounts; the said Law 1, paragraph: "it must be considered" with the following paragraph; Law 2, paragraph 1 in the Digest on guardianship and the distribution of accounts.</margin>
15. By this, he who has stolen property from the goods of the ward during the administration of the guardianship is held for double, to which is added the prosecution of the thing itself <note>original: "r" and "s"</note>.

<margin>t the said Law 1, at the end; Law 4 in the beginning in the Digest on guardianship and the distribution of accounts; it makes the final paragraph in the Institutes on the Atilian tutor.</margin>
16. And it is then competent, when the action of guardianship is also competent, that is, only when the guardianship is finished <note>original: "t"</note>.

<margin>u See the Reichsabscheidt (Imperial Decree) of Augsburg, year 1548, title "on wards and minors," paragraph 3, part 2, folio 59; follows the Electorate of the Palatinate Guardianship Ordinance, title 9; Arnoldus ab Haersolt in Adversaria of actions, part 4, action 22, number 5.</margin>
17. Which, however, is different today, since an account must be rendered every year of the administration <note>original: "u"</note>.

18. Actions akin to the former, inasmuch as they are born from administration and thus from quasi-contract, are the useful action of curatorship
